title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41:1–40)
hook: seven fat cows, seven thin; Joseph plans for famine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph in prison: a butler, a baker, and one request. Your line: remember me.

Two full years go by. Then the most powerful man in Egypt has a bad night. Pharaoh dreams he's standing by the Nile, and seven sleek, fat cows come up out of the river. Then seven thin, ugly ones come up and eat the fat ones, and look just as thin as before. He sleeps again and dreams of seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. In the morning he calls every wise man and magician in Egypt. Nobody can tell him what it means. And the butler, holding the cup, suddenly remembers something.
screen: `SEVEN FAT, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: The butler confesses: I remember my faults this day. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph at once, and Joseph shaves and changes his clothes. The young man who keeps losing his garments gets a new one. Pharaoh says, I hear you can interpret dreams. Joseph answers, in the King James Bible: "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The same move as in prison: not me, God. The two dreams are one. Seven good years of harvest are coming, then seven years of famine so severe the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, he says, because God has settled it. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives a plan. Set a wise man over the land. In the seven good years, store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities, kept for the famine. Don't spend all of the good years in the good years. Pharaoh asks his court: "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?" And he puts Joseph over all Egypt, second only to Pharaoh. This morning a forgotten prisoner; by the afternoon, he runs the country. Christians have read Joseph as a model of faith joined to practical wisdom: he trusts God with the future and still builds the barns. Here, giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan sit side by side.
screen: `SHAVED AND NEWLY CLOTHED.` · `IT IS NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.` · `SEVEN GOOD YEARS, SEVEN LEAN.` · `STORE A FIFTH FOR THE FAMINE.` · then, large: `A MAN IN WHOM THE SPIRIT OF GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Your fat years might be money, or energy, or time with someone who won't always be around; a lean season will likely come too: a hard stretch, a quiet one, getting older. Picture one small thing you could set aside now: money, yes, but also patience, friendship, rest. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom about it.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin, seven full ears and seven scorched: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine.
Your line: plan for the lean years. Seven good years, stored for seven hard ones. Day three hundred seventy, in the books.

howItsDone: Christians often point to Joseph's storehouses when teaching about stewardship and wise planning, and many church food banks and savings programs draw on this story.

original.note: Hebrew spelling of Pharaoh, from an Egyptian phrase meaning great house, first the palace, then the king.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph had a talent for reading dreams.
what it means: he gives God the credit, then turns a warning into a plan, and a forgotten prisoner runs Egypt by evening.
what a scholar hears: Pharaoh's dreams are set at the Nile, whose yearly flood decided whether Egypt ate. ancient Egyptian texts also remember famines, though none can be tied to Joseph.

chat.says: If Joseph trusted God about the famine, why bother storing grain?
options: In the story he does both: gives God the credit, then plans to store a fifth of the harvest.

chat.meaning: Joseph says the answer is God's, then gives a plan: store a fifth in the good years. Faith and practical wisdom sit side by side.

Nile.meaning: Egypt's great river, where Pharaoh saw the cows come up

Spirit of God.meaning: Pharaoh's words for what he saw at work in Joseph

notes: 'I remember my faults this day' (41:9) is near-KJV wording given without quotation marks; confirm.
Pharaoh from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ, 'great house': standard etymology; confirm.
Trapdoor: Egyptian famine texts exist (e.g. the later Famine Stela) but none can be linked to Joseph; confirm the phrasing is suitably cautious.
'A fifth' from 41:34. 'Second only to Pharaoh' from 41:40.
'By the afternoon he runs the country' is a narrative compression of the same audience; confirm acceptable.
Audit (10% sample): 'no tension between praying and planning' overstated the text, since Joseph is not shown praying in Genesis 41; now 'giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan'.
